Decision-Aligned Evaluation of
Uncertainty Quantification

Annika Schneider Tommy Rochussen Joshua Stiller Vincent Fortuin Affiliation: Technical University of Munich Affiliation: Helmholtz AI Affiliation: MCML Affiliation: Konrad Zuse School of Excellence in Reliable AI Affiliation: LMU Munich Affiliation: University of Technology Nuremberg
Abstract

Uncertainty estimates in machine learning are typically evaluated using generic metrics such as the negative log-likelihood and expected calibration error, yet good performance on such metrics does not necessarily imply high utility in downstream decisions. We introduce decision-alignment, a criterion that reveals which evaluation metrics meaningfully align with downstream utilities. Applying this framework, we show that many widely used uncertainty metrics are either misaligned with common decision problems or encode pathological prior beliefs about the downstream task. We then propose prior-weighted utility metrics, a special class of proper scoring rules that provides decision-aligned uncertainty evaluation. Across benchmark experiments and real-world case studies, our metrics consistently align with realized decision utility, while conventional metrics do not. Our results surface flaws in the current UQ evaluation protocol and offer a principled extension of existing metrics toward decision-relevant UQ evaluation.

1 Introduction

Uncertainty quantification (UQ) in machine learning (ML) is key for reliable decision-making. Probabilistic ML research aims to develop high-quality UQ methods, facilitating ML usage in safety-critical domains. How UQ quality is measured directly shapes which methods are developed, published, and deployed. Since the “true uncertainty” cannot be observed, UQ evaluation relies on surrogate metrics such as negative log-likelihood (NLL) or expected calibration error (ECE) [1, 2, 3]. However, good performance on such metrics does not necessarily imply high utility in downstream decisions [4, 5, 6]. We argue that UQ evaluation should reflect downstream decision utility directly.

In this paper, we take UQ evaluation as our object of study. We focus on general-purpose evaluation where no specific downstream task is fixed. Benchmarks guide progress in ML [7], so by restricting ourselves to generic measures such as the NLL and ECE at this stage, we risk leaving behind methods that do not excel on such metrics but are actually more useful in downstream applications.

In this work, we aim to improve the understanding of common UQ evaluation metrics and align UQ evaluation with decision-making. We make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    We introduce decision-alignment as a formal criterion to show that common UQ evaluation metrics either encode pathological priors or no coherent decision belief at all (Section 3).

  2. 2.

    Based on these findings, we propose prior-weighted utility metrics that capture a model’s value for downstream utilities (Section 4).

  3. 3.

    We demonstrate in classification and regression experiments that only prior-weighted utility metrics reliably align with real downstream utilities (Section 5).11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/fortuinlab/prior-weighted-utilities.

2 Related work

Here, we summarize the prior work most relevant to our contribution. In Appendix A, we comment in more detail on the scope of our work. Further studies that share similarities with our framework or goals are acknowledged in Appendix B.

Common UQ evaluation metrics in ML

Current UQ studies in ML primarily evaluate uncertainty through predictive accuracy and calibration metrics. Benchmarking studies such as those of Ovadia et al. [1], Nado et al. [8], and Basora et al. [3] typically assess models using NLL, Brier score (BS), ECE, and ranking-scores such as the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC). Among these metrics, proper scoring rules (PSRs) such as the NLL and BS are often considered favorable as they are minimized at the ground-truth predictive distribution, and hence encourage honest uncertainty estimates [9, 10]. In practice, however, the true distribution is unknown, such that we never know whether a model ever truly minimizes the score [11], limiting the value of properness in UQ benchmarking. While the benchmarking tools URSABench [2] and Neural Testbed [12] do incorporate decision-making and bandit-style evaluations respectively, these decision scenarios are artificial and simplified, limiting their transferability to the real-world. In contrast, our prior-weighted utility metrics are aligned with realistic downstream decisions in a principled manner.

Connection of PSRs & decisions

There is a well-known connection between PSRs and decision-making—every decision problem induces a PSR [13]. Further, in binary classification, any PSR can be expressed as a cost-weighted average over dichotomous decisions (under mild regularity conditions, see [14, 15, 16, 9, 10, 17]); a result that inspires our decision-alignment framework. Some regression PSRs can also be expressed in terms of decisions, e.g., the continuous ranked probability score and BS can be expressed as averages over thresholded decisions [9], but this relationship is less general than in classification [18]. These relationships give rise to the assumption that good performance on common PSRs relates to good performance in downstream decisions, but we refute this assumption through our decision-alignment criterion.

Connection between calibration & decisions

It is unclear whether better performance on calibration metrics leads to better decision-making. While some studies observed that good calibration implies good decisions [19, 20], others argue that metrics such as the ECE are flawed in terms of evaluating the usefulness of a model in downstream decisions [21, 22, 6]. There has been substantial recent work on more decision-centric notions of calibration which aim to provide approximate guarantees (up to some tolerance ε\varepsilon) for downstream decision utilities or restricted families of tasks [23, 24, 25, 26]. These approaches are primarily motivated by training or post-hoc adjustment, and have limited use for benchmarking since ε\varepsilon-guarantees do not allow for consistent ranking of two predictors—differences in downstream utility may lie within the approximation error. In contrast, our prior-weighted utilities are intentionally designed to provide consistent model rankings in terms of downstream utility and are therefore preferable in the context of benchmarking.

3 Implicit decision beliefs of UQ metrics

Standard UQ metrics are often justified axiomatically (e.g., through properness or calibration), but there is only a limited understanding of their implications for downstream utilities. We generalize the known connection between PSRs and decisions (see Section 2) to decision-alignment, allowing a systematic analysis of common UQ metrics in terms of decision utilities.

3.1 Decision-alignment of UQ metrics

We consider metrics MM and decision utilities UθU_{\theta}, parametrized by θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, that evaluate a prediction-label pair (𝒇,𝒚)(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}), where 𝒚=(y1,…,yn)∈𝒴n\boldsymbol{y}=(y_{1},\dots,y_{n})\in\mathcal{Y}^{n} and 𝒇=(f1,…,fn)∈𝒫n\boldsymbol{f}=(f_{1},\dots,f_{n})\in\mathcal{P}^{n}, n≥2n\geq 2, and 𝒴,𝒫\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{P} depend on the task and prediction model. We consider probabilistic predictions, so each f∈𝒫f\in\mathcal{P} encodes a distributional report over 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. For example, in probabilistic binary classification, 𝒴={0,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\} and 𝒫=[0,1]\mathcal{P}=[0,1], that is, the prediction model maps to the probability that a given instance has label 11. We restrict ourselves to prediction spaces 𝒫\mathcal{P} and utilities UθU_{\theta} such that for each f∈𝒫f\in\mathcal{P} a (not necessarily unique) Bayes act exists for UθU_{\theta}, that is, a decision that maximizes expected utility under ff. Without loss of generality, we say that smaller values of MM and larger values of UU correspond to better performance. Since the labels 𝒚\boldsymbol{y} are typically fixed, we use the notation22 2 Note that often, utility functions evaluate actions given labels, and we evaluate predictions given labels. To be precise, we define Uθ,y​(f)U_{\theta,y}(f) as the utility of the Bayes act under ff.

M𝒚​(𝒇):=M⁡(𝒇,𝒚)andUθ,𝒚​(𝒇):=Uθ​(𝒇,𝒚).M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}):=M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\quad\text{and}\quad U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}):=U_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}).
Definition 3.1 (Decision-alignment).

A metric MM is decision-aligned w.r.t. a decision family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} if there exists a prior π\pi s.t. for any fixed labels 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}, there exists a strictly increasing function h𝒚:Im⁡(M𝒚)→ℝh_{\boldsymbol{y}}:\mathrm{Im}(M_{\boldsymbol{y}})\to\mathbb{R} s.t.

h𝒚(M𝒚(𝒇))=∫Θ−Uθ,𝒚(𝒇)π(θ)dθ∀𝒇.h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\bigr)=\int_{\Theta}-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\,\pi(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta\quad\forall\boldsymbol{f}. (1)
Remark 3.2 (On the nature of π\pi).

In our framework, π\pi can be any nonnegative and nonzero measure on Θ\Theta. It does not need to be finite and, in particular, does not need to be a probability measure. We only require that the right-hand side of (1) is well-defined and finite. To simplify notation, we write π⁡(θ)​d​θ\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta for integration w.r.t. the measure π\pi, including absolutely continuous priors with density π⁡(θ)\pi(\theta), as well as purely atomic priors such as Dirac measures δ\delta. We use the term prior to highlight that π\pi encodes the metric’s implicit belief on the downstream utility’s parameter, and one can think of the right-hand side in (1) as the (negative) expected utility under θ∼π\theta\sim\pi. Thus, we introduce the notation

EUθ∼π,𝒚(𝒇):=∫Θ−Uθ,𝒚(𝒇)π(θ)dθ.EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}):=\int_{\Theta}-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\,\pi(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
Remark 3.3 (On the choice of our framework).

The reason why we defined our framework of the form (1) is two-fold:

(1) Metric-analysis: Expressing a metric MM through (1) reveals whether it implicitly anticipates some decision family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} under a prior π\pi. This helps us decide when and whether to use the metric, and to interpret model rankings under MM appropriately.

(2) Desirable metric property: Decision-alignment is a necessary and sufficient condition for strict order- and tie-preservation (see Proposition 3.4), and thus a naturally desirable metric property. Intuitively, a metric M\boldsymbol{M} is decision-aligned if and only if it ranks predictions exactly as expected utility under π\boldsymbol{\pi} would.

Proposition 3.4 (Decision-alignment ⇔\Leftrightarrow strict order- and tie-preservation).

Fix a decision family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} and a prior π\pi. Then, for any fixed 𝐲\boldsymbol{y}, the following statements are equivalent:

(I) MM is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} under π\pi.

(II) MM is strictly order-preserving and tie-preserving for {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} under π\pi, i.e., for all 𝐟1,𝐟2\boldsymbol{f}_{1},\boldsymbol{f}_{2},

M𝒚​(𝒇1)<M𝒚​(𝒇2)\displaystyle M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{1})<M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{2}) ⇒E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇1)<E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇2),\displaystyle\Rightarrow EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{1})<EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{2}),
M𝒚​(𝒇1)=M𝒚​(𝒇2)\displaystyle M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{1})=M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{2}) ⇒E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇1)=E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇2).\displaystyle\Rightarrow EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{1})=EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{2}).
Proof sketch.

(I)⇒\Rightarrow(II): Follows through strict monotonicity of h𝒚h_{\boldsymbol{y}}. (II)⇒\Rightarrow(I): Follows by defining h𝒚​(m)h_{\boldsymbol{y}}(m) as E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇)EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}) for any 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} with M𝒚​(𝒇)=mM_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})=m. We state the full proof in Section C.1. ∎

In other words, decision-aligned metrics rank models according to their expected utility in the respective downstream decision family. Further, any metric that is strictly order- and tie-preserving is also decision-aligned, so Definition 3.1 includes all metrics that fulfill these criteria. In Appendix D, we discuss the relationship between decision-aligned metrics and PSRs.

To understand what kind of metrics can be decision-aligned with respect to what types of utility families, we distinguish between pointwise-separable, coordinate-independent, and coordinate-dependent metrics/utilities.

Definition 3.5 (Pointwise-separability & coordinate-independence).

A metric/utility SS is pointwise-separable if there exists a measurable instance function ss s.t.33 3 This is essentially a stricter version of decomposable and non-decomposable losses [27], requiring the same instance function ss for each component ii.

S⁡(𝒇,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1ns⁡(fi,yi)S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}s(f_{i},y_{i}) (2)

Otherwise, SS is non-separable. SS is coordinate-independent if the change in SS through altering one prediction fif_{i} does not depend on the other coordinates, that is, for a,b∈𝒫a,b\in\mathcal{P} and 𝒓,𝒓′∈𝒫n−1\boldsymbol{r},\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}^{n-1}

S𝒚​((a,𝒓))<S𝒚​((b,𝒓))⇔S𝒚​((a,𝒓′))<S𝒚​((b,𝒓′)),S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((a,\boldsymbol{r}))<S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((b,\boldsymbol{r}))\Leftrightarrow S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((a,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}))<S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((b,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})),

and analogously for equality and opposite strict inequality.44 4 We write (fi,𝒓)(f_{i},\boldsymbol{r}) for the prediction vector with value fif_{i} at the ithi^{\text{th}} position and values 𝒓\boldsymbol{r} at the remaining n−1n-1 positions. Otherwise, SS is coordinate-dependent.

Note that each pointwise-separable metric/utility is also coordinate-independent: For a pointwise-separable SS, changing fif_{i} only affects s⁡(fi,yi)s(f_{i},y_{i}), which is independent of the remaining predictions. Next, we show that coordinate-dependent metrics (e.g., calibration or ranking metrics) can immediately be ruled out as decision-aligned with respect to pointwise-separable utility families.

Lemma 3.6 (Separability barrier).

If the utility UθU_{\theta} is pointwise-separable for every θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta and θ↦Uθ​(𝐟,𝐲)\theta\mapsto U_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) is integrable for all (𝐟,𝐲)(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}), then any metric MM that is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} (for some prior π\pi) must be coordinate-independent.

Proof sketch.

By exchanging the integral and pointwise sum on the right-hand side of (1), we get that h𝒚​(M𝒚​(𝒇))h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\bigr) is pointwise-separable, which requires MM to be coordinate-independent. We state the full proof in Section C.2. ∎

Note that the converse of Lemma 3.6 is not true: A coordinate-independent metric MM can be decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} even if every UθU_{\theta} is non-separable, as long as the non-separable parts cancel out in the integral (see Appendix E for an example).

We now analyze concrete examples of metric-decision pairings through the lens of decision-alignment. We consider decision tasks that arise naturally in applications and span both pointwise-separable and non-separable utilities—binary decisions (yes/no), selective prediction (only predict when sure enough), and top-kk selection (select a few items from a large candidate pool).

3.2 Classification

In this section, we consider probabilistic binary55 5 We generalize our analysis to multiclass classification in Section G.1. classification models f:𝒳→[0,1]f:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1], mapping from the input space 𝒳\mathcal{X} to the probability that the true label from the output space 𝒴={0,1}\mathcal{Y}=\{0,1\} is 1. As evaluation metrics, we consider the negative log-likelihood (NLL), Brier score (BS), accuracy (Acc), expected calibration error (ECE), maximum calibration error (MCE), area under the retention curve (R-AUC), and error detection (E-Det). We state the metric definitions in Appendix F, where we also show that the NLL, BS, and Acc are coordinate-independent, and the ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are coordinate-dependent. The results of this section are summarized on the left of Table 1.

3.2.1 Binary decision

We first consider a binary decision problem where an action in {0,1}\{0,1\} (e.g., {do not treat, treat}\{\text{do not treat, treat}\}) is taken based on the model’s predicted probability f⁡(x)=f∈[0,1]f(x)=f\in[0,1], x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} for the positive class (e.g., disease present). We assume zero cost for correct predictions and costs CFP,CFN>0C_{\text{FP}},C_{\text{FN}}>0 for false positive and false negative predictions. Without loss of generality, we normalize the costs as cFP=CFP/(CFP+CFN)c_{\text{FP}}=C_{\text{FP}}/(C_{\text{FP}}+C_{\text{FN}}) (so cFN=1−cFPc_{\text{FN}}=1-c_{\text{FP}}). For ease of notation, we write c=cFPc=c_{\text{FP}} in the following. With this setup, the Bayes act is to select action 11 whenever f>cf>c [28]. This allows us to write the pointwise utility of a prediction ff with true label y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} for a fixed cost c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1) as

uc​(f,y)=−y⁡(1−c)​𝟏f≤c−(1−y)​c​𝟏f>c.u_{c}(f,y)=-y(1-c)\boldsymbol{1}_{f\leq c}-(1-y)c\boldsymbol{1}_{f>c}.

Proposition 3.7 (Buja et al. [16]).

The NLL, BS, and Acc are decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uc}c∈(0,1)\{U_{c}\}_{c\in(0,1)} with

πNLL​(c)=1/(c⁡(1−c)),πBS=2,πAcc​(c)=2​δ0.5​(c)\pi_{\text{NLL}}(c)=1/(c(1-c)),\ \pi_{\text{BS}}=2,\ \pi_{\text{Acc}}(c)=2\delta_{0.5}(c)

While this decision-theoretic interpretation suggests that good performance on PSRs and Acc implies good decision-making, we would like to emphasize that the implicit priors of common PSRs are pathological.77 7 We characterize pathological priors as either (a) degenerate priors, (b) uninformative priors, or (c) priors that place unbounded mass on extreme regions where UQ is least needed. In many binary decisions, the cost of a false negative (e.g., missed disease) is much higher than the cost of a false positive (e.g., unnecessary treatment [28]). πNLL​(c)\pi_{\text{NLL}}(c) places unbounded mass on extreme regions, rewarding performance where one error type is essentially free and a trivial policy suffices. The BS weighs each c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1) equally, corresponding to an uninformative prior. πAcc​(c)\pi_{\text{Acc}}(c) is degenerate, expressing the strong assumption that the costs are perfectly symmetric. We visualize πNLL,πBS\pi_{\text{NLL}},\pi_{\text{BS}}, and πAcc\pi_{\text{Acc}} on the left of Figure G.1.

Since the ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are coordinate-dependent, we can directly follow from Lemma 3.6 that they are not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uc}c∈(0,1)\{U_{c}\}_{c\in(0,1)}.

Corollary 3.8.

The ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uc}c∈(0,1)\{U_{c}\}_{c\in(0,1)}.

3.2.2 Top-𝒌\boldsymbol{k} selection

Top-kk selection for k∈[n−1]:={1,…,n−1}k\in[n-1]:=\{1,\dots,n-1\} arises, for instance, in the context of recommender systems. As downstream utility, we use the established precision@kk metric (in line with, e.g., [29]),

Uk​(𝒇,𝒚)=1k​∑i∈𝒮k​(𝒇)yi,U_{k}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{k}(\boldsymbol{f})}y_{i},

where 𝒮k​(𝒇)\mathcal{S}_{k}(\boldsymbol{f}) is the index set of the selected instances according to the predicted scores.88 8 For 𝒮k​(𝒇)\mathcal{S}_{k}(\boldsymbol{f}) to be uniquely defined, one can choose a tie-breaking rule or restrict to 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} with unique entries. This can be interpreted as receiving equal reward (normalized to 1k\tfrac{1}{k}) for each correctly selected positive instance, and no reward for selecting negative instances. The Bayes act is to select the kk instances with the highest scores [30]. 𝑼𝒌\boldsymbol{U_{k}} is non-separable (whether an instance contributes to UkU_{k} depends on its rank relative to all other predictions, and therefore UkU_{k} cannot be written as a sum of independent terms), so we cannot leverage Lemma 3.6. Nevertheless, we are able to prove that none of the metrics we consider are decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uk}k∈[n−1]\{U_{k}\}_{k\in[n-1]}.

Proposition 3.9.

The NLL, BS, Acc, ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uk}k∈[n−1]\{U_{k}\}_{k\in[n-1]}.

Proof sketch.

The value of UkU_{k} is only influenced by the subset 𝒮k​(𝒇)\mathcal{S}_{k}(\boldsymbol{f}), and all metrics we consider evaluate on the entire dataset. One can find predictions 𝒇1,𝒇2\boldsymbol{f}_{1},\boldsymbol{f}_{2} that yield different metric values but leave the expected utility unchanged. We state the full proof in Section C.3. ∎

Remark 3.10 (Case k=nk=n).

When defining UkU_{k}, we excluded the trivial case of k=nk=n (select all data points). Note, however, that Acc actually equals UkU_{k} for k=nk=n. In other words, Acc is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uk}k∈[n]\{U_{k}\}_{k\in[n]} under the (pathological) prior π​(k)=δn​(k)\pi(k)=\delta_{n}(k).

3.3 Regression

In this section, we consider probabilistic univariate99 9 We generalize our analysis to multivariate regression in Section G.2. regression models. We assume a Gaussian predictive distribution1010 10 We assume a Gaussian distribution for simplicity, but any distribution with a well-defined mean and variance is admissible. and consider models of the form f:𝒳→ℝ×ℝ>0f:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{>0}, mapping from the input space 𝒳\mathcal{X} to the predictive mean μ∈ℝ\mu\in\mathbb{R} and predictive variance σ2∈ℝ>0\sigma^{2}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}, so f=(μ,σ2)f=(\mu,\sigma^{2}). The regression target is the true label y∈𝒴:=ℝy\in\mathcal{Y}:=\mathbb{R}. As evaluation metrics, we consider the NLL, mean squared error (MSE), ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det. We state the metric definitions in Appendix F, where we also show that the NLL and MSE are coordinate-independent, and the ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are coordinate-dependent. We summarize the results on the right of Table 1.

3.3.1 Selective prediction

In selective prediction, the decision-maker chooses an action in {predict,abstain}\{\text{predict},\text{abstain}\}, where selecting predict corresponds to issuing a point prediction y^\hat{y}, while abstain corresponds to deferring the decision (e.g., to a human expert). We assume squared loss for point predictions and a fixed abstention cost λ∈ℝ>0\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. With this setup, the Bayes act is to issue the predictive mean μ\mu whenever the predictive variance σ2\sigma^{2} is at most the abstention cost. This allows us to write the pointwise utility of a prediction f=(μ,σ2)f=(\mu,\sigma^{2}) with true outcome y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R} for a fixed abstention cost λ\lambda as

uλ​(f,y)=−(μ−y)2​ 1σ2≤λ−λ​ 1σ2>λ.u_{\lambda}(f,y)=-(\mu-y)^{2}\,\boldsymbol{1}_{\sigma^{2}\leq\lambda}-\lambda\,\boldsymbol{1}_{\sigma^{2}>\lambda}.

Once again, the dataset-level utility Uλ​(𝒇,𝒚)U_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) is defined as the average pointwise utility, so 𝑼𝝀\boldsymbol{U_{\lambda}} is pointwise-separable, and therefore the ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uλ}λ∈ℝ>0\{U_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}} by Lemma 3.6. We find that this also holds for the NLL and MSE.

Proposition 3.11.

The NLL, MSE, ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uλ}λ∈ℝ>0\{U_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}}.

Proof sketch.

The MSE only evaluates the point prediction μ\mu and is therefore insensitive to σ2\sigma^{2}, so improvements in UλU_{\lambda} through σ2\sigma^{2} cannot be measured. The NLL does exhibit the same form as UλU_{\lambda} after monotone transformation under a Pareto prior π\pi, but the expected utility diverges because π\pi goes to infinity for λ→0\lambda\to 0 too quickly, violating our requirements for a valid prior. For the coordinate-dependent metrics, we can apply Lemma 3.6. We state the full proof in Section C.4. ∎

Notably, the proof of Proposition 3.11 reveals that under minor additional assumptions, the NLL is decision-aligned w.r.t. the UλU_{\lambda}-family under a Pareto prior.

Proposition 3.12.

Fix any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and define 𝒫ε:={f=(μ,σ2)∣σ2>ε}\mathcal{P}_{\varepsilon}:=\{f=(\mu,\sigma^{2})\mid\sigma^{2}>\varepsilon\}. Consider only predictions 𝐟∈𝒫εn\boldsymbol{f}\in\mathcal{P}_{\varepsilon}^{n}. Then, the NLL is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uλ}λ∈ℝ>ε\{U_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{>\varepsilon}} under π⁡(λ)=ε​λ−2\pi(\lambda)=\varepsilon\lambda^{-2} and

h𝒚​(m)=2​ε​m−ε​log⁡(2​π​ε)∀𝒚.h_{\boldsymbol{y}}(m)=2\varepsilon m-\varepsilon\log(2\pi\varepsilon)\quad\forall\boldsymbol{y}.
Proof sketch.

When restricting to λ,σi2>ε\lambda,\sigma_{i}^{2}>\varepsilon for all ii, we avoid the divergence issues from Proposition 3.11 and decision-alignment holds. We state the full proof in Section C.5. ∎

Note that this Pareto​(1,ε)\text{Pareto}(1,\varepsilon) prior is pathological, as it places more weight on λ\lambda the smaller λ\lambda is. In other words, it anticipates almost negligible abstention costs. We visualize the Pareto prior on the right of Figure G.1, alongside the Dirac prior for the case λ=∞\lambda=\infty discussed below.

Remark 3.13 (Case λ=∞\lambda=\infty).

When defining UλU_{\lambda}, we excluded the trivial case of λ=∞\lambda=\infty (always predict). Note, however, that the MSE actually equals UλU_{\lambda} for λ=∞\lambda=\infty. In other words, the MSE is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uλ}λ∈ℝ>0∪{∞}\{U_{\lambda}\}_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}} under the (pathological) prior π⁡(λ)=δ∞​(λ)\pi(\lambda)=\delta_{\infty}(\lambda).

3.3.2 Top-𝒌\boldsymbol{k} selection

Given predictions 𝒇=(𝝁,𝝈𝟐)\boldsymbol{f}=(\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\sigma^{2}}) and labels 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}, we consider a mean–variance trade-off of the form

Uϕ​(𝒇,𝒚)=1k​∑i∈𝒮ϕ​(𝒇)(yi−γ​σi2),U_{\phi}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}_{\phi}(\boldsymbol{f})}(y_{i}-\gamma\sigma_{i}^{2}),

where ϕ=(k,γ)∈Φ:=[n−1]×ℝ>0\phi=(k,\gamma)\in\Phi:=[n-1]\times\mathbb{R}_{>0}, and γ\gamma controls the degree of risk aversion. The Bayes act is to select the top-kk instances according to the score μi−γ​σi2\mu_{i}-\gamma\sigma_{i}^{2}. This yields a selection policy that trades off between predicted benefit and uncertainty. As in classification, we can show that none of the metrics we consider is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uϕ}ϕ∈Φ\{U_{\phi}\}_{\phi\in\Phi}.

Proposition 3.14.

The NLL, MSE, ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uϕ}ϕ∈Φ\{U_{\phi}\}_{\phi\in\Phi}.

Proof sketch.

As in classification, the value of the utility is only influenced by the top-kk subset, and all metrics we consider evaluate on the entire dataset. We state the full proof in Section C.6. ∎

4 Prior-weighted utility metrics

The key takeaway from Section 3 is that common UQ evaluation metrics either encode implausible decision beliefs or do not reflect decision utility at all. In other words, current UQ benchmarks silently optimize for the wrong downstream world. In pursuit of a better UQ evaluation protocol, we propose prior-weighted utility (PWU) metrics which are, by definition, decision-aligned and encode plausible prior beliefs about downstream decisions.1111 11 Appendix H states a structured PWU documentation, similar to model cards [31], alongside a broader impact statement.

4.1 PWU construction

To define a PWU metric, we select a decision family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} and a plausible prior π\pi such that E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇)<∞EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})<\infty for all (𝒇,𝒚)(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}). To align the PWU metric MπM_{\pi} with {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta}, we apply Equation 1 directly with h𝒚=idh_{\boldsymbol{y}}=\mathrm{id} for all 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}:

Mπ(𝒇,𝒚):=∫Θ−Uθ(𝒇,𝒚)π(θ)dθ.M_{\pi}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\int_{\Theta}-U_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\,\pi(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta. (4)

We propose a PWU metric for each decision problem analyzed in Section 3, obtaining

Mπc​(𝒇,𝒚)\displaystyle M_{\pi_{c}}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) =∫01−Uc(𝒇,𝒚)πc(c)dc,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}-U_{c}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\,\pi_{c}(c)\,\mathrm{d}c,\qquad Mπλ​(𝒇,𝒚)\displaystyle M_{\pi_{\lambda}}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) =∫0∞−Uλ(𝒇,𝒚)πλ(λ)dλ,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}-U_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\,\pi_{\lambda}(\lambda)\,\mathrm{d}\lambda,
Mπk​(𝒇,𝒚)\displaystyle M_{\pi_{k}}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) =∑k=1n−1−Uk(𝒇,𝒚)πk(k),\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}-U_{k}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\,\pi_{k}(k),\qquad Mπϕ​(𝒇,𝒚)\displaystyle M_{\pi_{\phi}}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) =∫0∞∑k=1n−1−Uϕ(𝒇,𝒚)πϕ(ϕ)dϕ.\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}-U_{\phi}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\,\pi_{\phi}(\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\phi.

In Figure 1, we visualize the priors we choose for our experiments. In Appendix I, we justify them explicitly and provide some general guidance on prior elicitation. Note that constructing a PWU metric is a general method that can be applied to a broader set of decisions (and priors) than just those considered in this paper. Since each metric corresponds to a single decision family, it is advisable to use a variety of PWU metrics in UQ benchmarking to test models across different decision contexts.

4.2 Metric properties

The purpose of our PWU metrics is to evaluate UQ in terms of downstream decision utility. Thus, we intentionally defined them to be decision-aligned with their corresponding utility family.

Proposition 4.1 (PWU metrics are decision-aligned).

Pick any decision family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} and a prior π\pi over Θ\Theta. Then, the resulting PWU metric MπM_{\pi} is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} under π\pi.

Proof.

Follows by comparing the PWU definition (4) to Definition 3.1 with h𝒚=idh_{\boldsymbol{y}}=\mathrm{id} for all 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}. ∎

Recall that decision-alignment is equivalent to strict order- and tie-preservation. Hence, PWU metrics offer a principled and decision-theoretic value for UQ benchmarking. Furthermore, using a PWU metric does not sacrifice properness—all PWU metrics are proper, and even strictly proper if the Bayes act for each UθU_{\theta} is unique for all 𝒇\boldsymbol{f}.

Proposition 4.2 (PWU metrics are proper).

Pick any decision family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} and a corresponding prior π\pi, and assume ∫Θ𝔼𝐘∼𝐩​[|Uθ,𝐘​(𝐟)|]​π​(θ)​𝑑θ<∞\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[|U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f})|\right]\,\pi(\theta)\,\mathrm{d}\theta<\infty for all (𝐟,𝐲)(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}). Then, the resulting PWU metric MπM_{\pi} is a PSR, and it is strictly proper if the Bayes acts for each UθU_{\theta} are unique under all 𝐟\boldsymbol{f}.

Proof.

MπM_{\pi} is decision-aligned by Proposition 4.1 and, by comparing (4) to Definition 3.1, we have h𝒚=idh_{\boldsymbol{y}}=\mathrm{id} for all 𝒚\boldsymbol{y}. Therefore, we can apply Proposition D.1 with a=1,b=0a=1,b=0 and conclude that MπM_{\pi} is proper (and strictly proper if the Bayes acts for each UθU_{\theta} are unique under all 𝒇\boldsymbol{f}). ∎

Our PWU metrics do not come without limitations (see also Appendix H). No single PWU can cover all downstream objectives, so we recommend using a variety of PWUs in UQ evaluation. Furthermore, PWU priors may be misspecified. However, in Section J.3 we show empirically that PWU metrics retain strong positive utility-alignment even under severe prior perturbation, in stark contrast to the brittleness of conventional metrics under their pathological implicit priors. These results highlight PWUs’ suitability for general-purpose UQ benchmarking.

5 Experiments

5.1 Controlled experiments on benchmark datasets

We implement ten binary classification and ten univariate regression models1212 12 We present results for the multiclass and multivariate settings in Appendix K. and evaluate these models on five datasets each. The experiments aim to measure how well the model ranking of each metric MM aligns with the performance on downstream utilities. We use all metrics analyzed in Section 3 in addition to our PWU metrics, and compare their rankings to the four decision utilities UθU_{\theta}, θ∈{c,k,λ,ϕ}\theta\in\{c,k,\lambda,\phi\} from Section 3. We then assess how well the model rankings of the metrics align with the model rankings of the utilities using Kendall’s τ\tau. We repeat this procedure on 100 differently sampled test sets to quantify the results’ variability. In Figure 2, we report our results as boxplots1313 13 The boxplots show the median, 25th and 75th percentiles via boxes, and 5th, 95th percentiles via whiskers. and state the exact numbers in Tables J.1, J.2, J.3, J.4. We detail our chosen models, datasets, experimental setup, and general reproducibility in Appendix J. Overall, even though some conventional metrics are decision-aligned, we see that their pathological priors negatively impact their utility-alignment. Crucially, in top-kk selection and selective prediction, most of the common metrics exhibit little to no utility alignment, rendering them largely uninformative for downstream decision-making. In contrast, our PWU metrics align best with their corresponding utility family.

5.2 Applied case studies

While the above experiments consider the same utilities as our PWUs, we now deviate from this setup and implement three applied case studies. In our first case study, we consider a wind farm operator who wants to sell electricity in the day-ahead market, where bids must be placed one day in advance. If the actual wind power production deviates from the bid, they risk a penalty for the resulting shortfall or surplus, as, in both cases, the electricity grid’s supply-demand balance needs to be restored. We follow the setup from Bruninx et al. [32], who derive an optimal bidding policy that resembles a selective prediction problem: bid only when the wind power forecast is sufficiently certain. The utility (payoff) is market-dependent for every bid/abstention and unknown in advance, deviating significantly from our controlled setup. We explain the case study in more detail in Section J.2 and show the results in Table 2 and Figure J.5. In this real-life setup, none of the conventional UQ metrics have a stable positive bidding utility alignment, again showcasing how disconnected generic metrics are from real-world tasks. In contrast, our PWU metrics exhibit the strongest utility alignment.

In our remaining two case studies (see Section J.2), we consider the tasks of credit approval and peer-to-peer lending, again using real-world economic payoffs as utility functions. We observe once more that our PWU metrics reliably align with the decision utility—despite the fact that some decision parameters differ strongly from our chosen PWU priors (see Figure J.4). This demonstrates that PWU metrics remain robust under prior misspecification, a finding further supported by our systematic sensitivity analysis (see Section J.3).

6 Conclusion

We introduced decision-alignment as a criterion that connects uncertainty evaluation metrics to downstream decision utility and used it to diagnose that many standard UQ metrics are either misaligned with common decision problems or encode pathological implicit priors. Motivated by this insight, we proposed PWU metrics, a principled class of decision-aligned PSRs that enable utility-relevant benchmarking. Across benchmark datasets and real-world case studies, PWU metrics consistently produce model rankings that better reflect realized decision utility than conventional UQ metrics. Our results suggest that the dominant practice of evaluating UQ with generic metrics can be systematically misleading when the goal is to support downstream decisions. Instead, we claim that meaningful progress in probabilistic ML requires evaluating models with a variety of PWU metrics,1414 14 We provide our concrete recommendations for future UQ benchmarking that result from this paper in Appendix L. so that UQ benchmarks bring methods to light that enable reliable decision-making.

Appendix A Scope of the paper

This appendix clarifies the scope of our work, which we term first-order UQ evaluation. Throughout this paper, a probabilistic prediction refers to a single distribution over the label space; we call such an object a first-order probabilistic prediction. In probabilistic binary classification, this is a single f∈[0,1]f\in[0,1] encoding Pr⁡(Y=1∣X)\Pr(Y=1\mid X); in regression, it is a single distribution over 𝒴\mathcal{Y} such as a Gaussian 𝒩⁡(μ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^{2}). This is the object almost universally produced and evaluated in probabilistic ML benchmarks [1, 8, 3], and the object for which all metrics we analyze (NLL, BS, MSE, Acc, ECE, MCE, R-AUC, E-Det) are defined.

A separate strand of the literature studies second-order probabilistic predictions: objects that take the form of a distribution over distributions. There are several reasons we restrict our scope to first-order evaluation. First, our work is positioned as a response to the current mainstream UQ evaluation literature (see Sections 1 and 2), which consistently uses metrics defined on first-order probabilistic predictions. Second, there is no broadly accepted evaluation protocol for second-order UQ to begin with [33, 34]. Many studies even evaluate the marginal predictive (see, e.g., [35, 36]), which is again first-order UQ and our analysis readily applies. Third, even if future research shifts more strongly toward second-order probabilistic predictions—a development we would welcome—we expect first-order evaluation to remain important for two reasons: interpretability—a single predictive distribution is substantially easier to communicate, visualize, and reason about than a distribution over distributions; and decision-theoretic use—Bayes-optimal actions under expected utility maximization are defined with respect to a single predictive distribution. Even models that maintain second-order beliefs internally are typically marginalized to a first-order posterior predictive distribution at decision time, so first-order quality remains the immediate driver of realized decision utility in most downstream pipelines.

Nevertheless, extending decision-aligned evaluation to second-order predictions is an interesting and important direction which we leave for future work.

Appendix B Omitted related work

Ehm et al. [18] study the evaluation and ranking of point forecasts through consistent scoring functions for functionals (e.g., quantiles). Similar to our decision-alignment, they consider consistency towards the functional of interest. They prove an order sensitivity result that resembles our Proposition 3.4, however, they order point forecasts and associated scores, while we order scores and utilities of distributional reports. In addition, they show only one direction (consistency implies order sensitivity) and consider only inequalities, whereas we show that decision-alignment is equivalent to strict order and tie preservation. Further, Ehm et al. [18] also discuss the decision-theoretic interpretation of binary decisions for PSRs and propose to use Murphy diagrams to evaluate and rank forecasts when the downstream task is unknown. As in our approach, they do not commit to a single decision parameter θ\theta. Murphy diagrams plot the score value over varying θ\theta, whereas we set plausible prior π⁡(θ)\pi(\theta) and report the corresponding (scalar) integral value. In addition, we do not restrict ourselves to an inherent downstream task like binary decisions in binary classification, but offer several decision-specific metrics for several tasks.

Bradley and Schwartz [37] also introduce a general framework tailored to ensemble weather forecasts, which is used to interpret known metrics. In their setup, probabilistic forecasts ff for a continuous variable YY are mapped to probability forecasts for threshold events of the form Y≤yY\leq y, and forecast quality is studied as a function Q⁡(y)Q(y) of the threshold. Within this framework, several standard verification scores (e.g., the continuous ranked probability skill score) are shown to correspond to weighted averages of the forecast quality function over thresholds. Our decision-alignment framework is more general, allowing metric interpretation with respect to any given (integrable) utility family and is theoretically motivated through strict order and tie preservation in terms of expected downstream utility.

Shahroudi et al. [38] propose to learn a proxy evaluation function for a known downstream task, motivated by the fact that evaluating the downstream utility can be costly. While their framework is termed evaluation alignment, similarly to our decision-alignment, the concepts differ substantially: In evaluation alignment, the decision loss needs to be known and is approximated with a learned PSR, while we propose general-purpose metrics for general-purpose evaluation where no specific downstream task is anticipated.

Ferrer and Ramos [6] advocate the use of expected PSRs (ESPRs), which are also defined as weighted integrals over a cost function (i.e., negative utility), but differ from our work in the sense that Ferrer and Ramos [6] only consider classification with pointwise classification cost. They neither analyze other metrics in terms of such an integral representation nor propose concrete new weight functions (i.e., priors), nor consider other utilities. The focus of the paper is rather to demonstrate that such ESPRs are superior to calibration metrics for UQ evaluation.

Pic et al. [11] propose another metric framework for probabilistic weather forecasts, specific to PSRs, based on aggregation (combining PSRs through a finite weighted sum) and transformation (transform forecasts and labels before applying the PSR). This is a different framework than decision-alignment—we do not require a transformation and our aggregation step (prior-weighted integral) is more general.

Also, Derr and Williamson [39] introduce a general framework for expressing evaluation metrics that represents metrics as the average realized value of gambles drawn from a predefined set. Their framework aims to unify a wide range of existing evaluation metrics by elucidating their structural relationships. In contrast, our work is not primarily concerned with unification, but with analyzing when and how metrics are informative for downstream decision-making.

Flores et al. [40] also build on the Schervish representation [15] to propose evaluation metrics for binary classifiers that reflect clinical priorities. Similarly, Flores et al. [41] propose to use a clipped variant of the Brier score to evaluate binary classifiers to better reflect decision-relevant thresholds. These works are conceptually a special case of our PWU metrics.

Proof.

h𝒚(M𝒚(𝒇))=∫Θ−1n∑i=1nuθ(fi,yi)π(θ)dθ=1n∑i=1n∫Θ−uθ(fi,yi)π(θ)dθ.h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\bigr)=\int_{\Theta}-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{\theta}(f_{i},y_{i})\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\int_{\Theta}-u_{\theta}(f_{i},y_{i})\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta.

Define the instance function s(fi,yi):=∫Θ−uθ(fi,yi)π(θ)dθs(f_{i},y_{i}):=\int_{\Theta}-u_{\theta}(f_{i},y_{i})\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta, then the above equation reads

h𝒚​(M𝒚​(𝒇))=1n​∑i=1ns⁡(fi,yi).h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\bigr)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}s(f_{i},y_{i}).

Define S𝒚​(𝒇):=1n​∑i=1ns⁡(fi,yi)S_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}s(f_{i},y_{i}), which is (by the form of its definition) pointwise-separable and hence also coordinate-independent, so, for a,b∈𝒫a,b\in\mathcal{P} and 𝒓,𝒓′∈𝒫n−1\boldsymbol{r},\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{P}^{n-1},

S𝒚​((a,𝒓))<S𝒚​((b,𝒓))⇔S𝒚​((a,𝒓′))<S𝒚​((b,𝒓′)),S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((a,\boldsymbol{r}))<S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((b,\boldsymbol{r}))\Leftrightarrow S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((a,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}))<S_{\boldsymbol{y}}((b,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})),

and because h𝒚​(M𝒚​(𝒇))=S𝒚​(𝒇)h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\bigr)=S_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}),

h𝒚​(M𝒚​((a,𝒓)))<h𝒚​(M𝒚​((b,𝒓)))⇔h𝒚​(M𝒚​((a,𝒓′)))<h𝒚​(M𝒚​((b,𝒓′))).h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}((a,\boldsymbol{r}))\bigr)<h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}((b,\boldsymbol{r}))\bigr)\Leftrightarrow h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}((a,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}))\bigr)<h_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl(M_{\boldsymbol{y}}((b,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}))\bigr).

Note that the corresponding expected utilities still match, even for a random tie-breaking rule, since the utility only depends on 𝟎\boldsymbol{0} and 𝝈𝟐\boldsymbol{\sigma^{2}}. Under 𝒇1\boldsymbol{f}_{1} we have e1=0e_{1}=0 and ei=1e_{i}=1 for i≥2i\geq 2, and the unique point with e=0e=0 has uncertainty score s⁡(v1)s(v_{1}) while every point with e=1e=1 has uncertainty score s⁡(vn)s(v_{n}). Since s⁡(v1)<s⁡(vn)s(v_{1})<s(v_{n}), all positives have strictly larger scores than all negatives, hence E-Det𝟎​(𝒇1)=−1\text{E-Det}_{\boldsymbol{0}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{1})=-1. Under 𝒇2\boldsymbol{f}_{2} we have e1=1e_{1}=1 and ei=0e_{i}=0 for i≥2i\geq 2, so the unique positive has score s⁡(v1)s(v_{1}) while all negatives have score s⁡(vn)s(v_{n}), implying E-Det𝟎​(𝒇2)=0\text{E-Det}_{\boldsymbol{0}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{2})=0.

In all cases, we obtain a contradiction. Therefore no such prior π\pi can exist, and MM is not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uϕ}ϕ∈Φ\{U_{\phi}\}_{\phi\in\Phi}. ∎

Appendix D Relationship between decision-alignment and properness

In this section, we prove that many decision-aligned metrics (those where the transformations h𝒚h_{\boldsymbol{y}} are affine) are proper. Note, however, that the converse is not true. While any PSR MM is decision-aligned to some decision-family, which we can simply define as Uθ=θ​MU_{\theta}=\theta M (and considering π​(θ)=δ1​(θ)\pi(\theta)=\delta_{1}(\theta)), a PSR is not decision-aligned to every utility family. We discuss several such examples in this paper (for example, the NLL is not decision-aligned w.r.t. the top-kk utility family).

Proposition D.1 (Decision-alignment with affine h𝒚h_{\boldsymbol{y}} ⇒\Rightarrow properness).

Suppose that the metric MM is decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} under π\pi with transformations h𝐲h_{\boldsymbol{y}}, and assume ∫Θ𝔼𝐘∼𝐩​[|Uθ,𝐘​(𝐟)|]​π​(θ)​𝑑θ<∞\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[|U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f})|\right]\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta<\infty for all (𝐟,𝐲)(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}). Further, assume there exists a constant a>0a>0 and a function b:𝒴n→ℝb:\mathcal{Y}^{n}\to\mathbb{R} s.t.

h𝒚​(m)=a​m+b⁡(𝒚)for all ​𝒚.h_{\boldsymbol{y}}(m)=am+b(\boldsymbol{y})\quad\text{for all }\boldsymbol{y}.

Then, MM is a PSR. If, in addition, the Bayes acts for each UθU_{\theta} are unique under all 𝐟\boldsymbol{f}, then MM is strictly proper.

Proof.

Define S⁡(𝒇,𝒚):=E​Uθ∼π,𝒚​(𝒇)S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}). By Dawid and Musio [13], we know that −Uθ,𝒚​(𝒇)-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}) is a PSR for all θ\theta. We first show that this implies that S⁡(𝒇,𝒚)S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) is a PSR as well. Denote by 𝒑\boldsymbol{p} the true distribution on 𝒴n\mathcal{Y}^{n}. By definition of properness, it holds for all predictions 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} that

𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[−Uθ,𝒀​(𝒑)]≤𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[−Uθ,𝒀​(𝒇)]for all ​θ∈Θ.\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{p})\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\right]\quad\text{for all }\theta\in\Theta.

Multiplying by the positive π⁡(θ)\pi(\theta) and integrating both sides w.r.t. θ\theta gives

∫Θ𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[−Uθ,𝒀​(𝒑)]​π​(θ)​𝑑θ≤∫Θ𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[−Uθ,𝒀​(𝒇)]​π​(θ)​𝑑θ,\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{p})\right]\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta\leq\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\right]\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta,

where the integrals exist by assumption. By Fubini-Tonelli (again using the assumed finiteness of expectations),

∫Θ𝔼𝒀∼𝒑[−Uθ,𝒀(𝒇)]π(θ)dθ=𝔼𝒀∼𝒑[∫Θ−Uθ,𝒀(𝒇)π(θ)dθ]=𝔼𝒀∼𝒑[S(𝒇,𝒀)].\int_{\Theta}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\right]\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[\int_{\Theta}-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f})\pi(\theta)\mathrm{d}\theta\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{Y})\right].

With the same equality on 𝒑\boldsymbol{p} instead of 𝒇\boldsymbol{f}, we get

𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[S⁡(𝒑,𝒀)]≤𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[S⁡(𝒇,𝒀)],\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[S(\boldsymbol{p},\boldsymbol{Y})\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}\left[S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{Y})\right],

which shows that S⁡(𝒇,𝒚)S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) is itself a PSR. Now, since

aM(𝒇,𝒚)+b(𝒚)=EUθ∼π,𝒚⇔M(𝒇,𝒚)=1aEUθ∼π,𝒚−1ab(𝒚),aM(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})+b(\boldsymbol{y})=EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}\ \ \Leftrightarrow\ \ M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{a}EU_{\theta\sim\pi,\boldsymbol{y}}-\frac{1}{a}b(\boldsymbol{y}),

we have for any prediction 𝒇\boldsymbol{f},

𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[M⁡(𝒇,𝒀)]=1a​𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[S⁡(𝒇,𝒀)]−1a​𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[b⁡(𝒀)],\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}[M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{Y})]=\frac{1}{a}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}[S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{Y})]-\frac{1}{a}\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}[b(\boldsymbol{Y})],

so the set of minimizers of 𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[M​(𝒇,𝒀)]\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}[M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{Y})] coincides with that of 𝔼𝒀∼𝒑​[S​(𝒇,𝒀)]\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{Y}\sim\boldsymbol{p}}[S(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{Y})]. Thus, MM is proper. If finally the Bayes acts for UθU_{\theta} are unique under all 𝒇\boldsymbol{f}, −Uθ,𝒚​(𝒇)-U_{\theta,\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}) is a strict PSR, all inequalities become strict inequalities, and MM will be a strict PSR. ∎

Appendix E Counterexample for the converse relation of Lemma 3.6

Consider 𝒫=𝒴=ℝ\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{Y}=\mathbb{R}. Define the pointwise-separable (and with this also coordinate-independent) metric

M⁡(𝒇,𝒚):=1n​∑i=1n(fi−yi)2.M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(f_{i}-y_{i})^{2}.

Let Θ={−1,+1}\Theta=\{-1,+1\} and fix the prior π⁡(+1)=π⁡(−1)=12\pi(+1)=\pi(-1)=\tfrac{1}{2}. Define the non-separable functional h⁡(𝒇,𝒚):=𝟏f1>f2h(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\boldsymbol{1}_{f_{1}>f_{2}}, which depends on the joint ordering of (f1,f2)(f_{1},f_{2}) and hence is not pointwise-separable. Now define a utility family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} by

U+1​(𝒇,𝒚):=−M⁡(𝒇,𝒚)−h⁡(𝒇,𝒚),U−1​(𝒇,𝒚):=−M⁡(𝒇,𝒚)+h⁡(𝒇,𝒚).U_{+1}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=-M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})-h(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}),\qquad U_{-1}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=-M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})+h(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}).

Then both U+1U_{+1} and U−1U_{-1} are non-separable (because of the ±h\pm h term), yet

∫Θ−Uθ(𝒇,𝒚)dπ(θ)\displaystyle\int_{\Theta}-U_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\mathrm{d}\pi(\theta) =12​(−U+1​(𝒇,𝒚))+12​(−U−1​(𝒇,𝒚))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(-U_{+1}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\bigr)+\frac{1}{2}\bigl(-U_{-1}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\bigr)
=12​(M⁡(𝒇,𝒚)+h⁡(𝒇,𝒚))+12​(M⁡(𝒇,𝒚)−h⁡(𝒇,𝒚))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})+h(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\bigr)+\frac{1}{2}\bigl(M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})-h(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\bigr)
=M⁡(𝒇,𝒚).\displaystyle=M(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}).

Hence, MM is decision-aligned w.r.t. the family {Uθ}θ∈Θ\{U_{\theta}\}_{\theta\in\Theta} under π\pi, even though every UθU_{\theta} in the family is non-separable.

Appendix F Omitted metric definitions

In this section, we define all metrics used in this paper and prove for each metric whether it is coordinate-independent or not. We start by defining each metric and giving a short intuition of why they are coordinate-(in)dependent. At the bottom of this section, we state a proposition, where we formally prove these intuitions.

Negative log-likelihood (NLL)

For binary classification, the pointwise NLL is defined as

lNLL​(f,y)=−y​log⁡(f)−(1−y)​log⁡(1−f),l_{\text{NLL}}(f,y)=-y\log(f)-(1-y)\log(1-f),

and for regression (f=(μ,σ2)f=(\mu,\sigma^{2})), we use the Gaussian NLL,

lNLL​(f,y)=12​log⁡(2​π​σ2)+(y−μ)22​σ2.l_{\text{NLL}}(f,y)=\tfrac{1}{2}\log(2\pi\sigma^{2})+\tfrac{(y-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}.

The dataset-level loss is defined as the average,

NLL​(𝒇,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1nlNLL​(fi,yi).\text{NLL}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{\text{NLL}}(f_{i},y_{i}).

Thus, by definition, the NLL is pointwise-separable, hence also coordinate-independent. Further, the NLL is a PSR [9].

Brier score (BS)

The pointwise BS is defined as

lBS​(f,y)=(f−y)2,l_{\text{BS}}(f,y)=(f-y)^{2},

and the dataset-level loss is defined as the average,

BS​(𝒇,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1nlBS​(fi,yi).\text{BS}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{\text{BS}}(f_{i},y_{i}).

Thus, by definition, the BS is pointwise-separable, hence also coordinate-independent. Further, the BS is a PSR [9].

Accuracy (Acc)

Accuracy (Acc) is conventionally defined as the ratio of correctly classified instances when using a generic decision threshold of 0.50.5. To conform with our notion that smaller metrics correspond to better performance, we consider the negative conventional accuracy as our Acc. With this, it is the sample average of the pointwise decision 0-1 loss, the indicator function of a false classification of any kind, minus 11, i.e.,

l0-1​(f,y)=y​𝟏f≤0.5+(1−y)​𝟏f>0.5,\displaystyle l_{\text{0-1}}(f,y)=y\boldsymbol{1}_{f\leq 0.5}+(1-y)\boldsymbol{1}_{f>0.5},
Acc​(𝒑,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1nl0-1​(pi,yi)−1.\displaystyle\text{Acc}(\boldsymbol{p},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{\text{0-1}}(p_{i},y_{i})-1.

Thus, by definition, Acc is pointwise-separable, hence also coordinate-independent, however, the Acc is not a PSR [9].

Mean squared error (MSE)

The pointwise mean squared error (MSE) is the squared-error loss, defined as

lMSE​(f,y):=(μ−y)2,l_{\text{MSE}}(f,y):=(\mu-y)^{2},

where f=(μ,σ2)f=(\mu,\sigma^{2}), and the dataset MSE is

MSE​(𝒇,𝒚):=1n​∑i=1nlMSE​(fi,yi).\text{MSE}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}l_{\text{MSE}}(f_{i},y_{i}).

Thus, by definition, the MSE is pointwise-separable, hence also coordinate-independent. The MSE only evaluates the predictive mean, not the full Gaussian predictive distribution, and can therefore not be considered proper in terms of the full probabilistic report 𝒇∈𝒫\boldsymbol{f}\in\mathcal{P}.

Expected calibration error (ECE)

A widely used empirical calibration metric in binary classification is the ECE, which measures the discrepancy between empirical frequencies and stated probabilities (aka calibration) within bins of the prediction space. Formally, fix a binning scheme ℬ={B1,…,Bm}\mathcal{B}=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{m}\} that partitions [0,1][0,1]. The ECE is defined as

ECE​(𝒇,𝒚):=∑j=1mnjn​|freq​(Bj)−conf​(Bj)|,\text{ECE}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\frac{n_{j}}{n}\bigl|\text{freq}(B_{j})-\text{conf}(B_{j})\bigr|,

where njn_{j} is the number of indices ii s.t. fi∈Bjf_{i}\in B_{j}, freq(Bj)=1nj∑i:fi∈Bjyi\text{freq}(B_{j})=\tfrac{1}{n_{j}}\sum_{i:\,f_{i}\in B_{j}}y_{i}, and conf(Bj)=1nj∑i:fi∈Bjfi\text{conf}(B_{j})=\tfrac{1}{n_{j}}\sum_{i:\,f_{i}\in B_{j}}f_{i}. We use 1010 equally spaced bins. The ECE is not a PSR [6]. The ECE is coordinate-dependent, since it couples coordinates through bin membership and bin statistics.

To use the ECE in regression, we follow Cui et al. [42], who assess calibration of regression models through nominal coverage levels α1,…,αm∈(0,1)\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{m}\in(0,1) and the corresponding Gaussian prediction intervals. We use α∈{0.5,0.8,0.9,0.95}\alpha\in\{0.5,0.8,0.9,0.95\}. Let α^j​((𝝁,𝝈2),𝒚)\hat{\alpha}_{j}((\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}),\boldsymbol{y}) denote the empirical miscoverage of the (1−αj)(1-\alpha_{j})-level prediction interval. Then, the empirical regression ECE is defined as

ECE​((𝝁,𝝈2),𝒚):=1m​∑j=1m|α^j​((𝝁,𝝈2),𝒚)−αj|.\text{ECE}((\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}),\boldsymbol{y}):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\bigl|\hat{\alpha}_{j}((\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}),\boldsymbol{y})-\alpha_{j}\bigr|.

As in the binary classification case, the regression ECE is not a PSR and coordinate-dependent.

Maximum calibration error (MCE)

The MCE measures the worst-case deviation between empirical frequencies and stated probabilities across bins of the prediction space. Using the same notation as for ECE, the MCE is defined as

MCE​(𝒇,𝒚):=maxj∈{1,…,m}⁡|freq​(Bj)−conf​(Bj)|.\text{MCE}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\max_{j\in\{1,\dots,m\}}\bigl|\text{freq}(B_{j})-\text{conf}(B_{j})\bigr|.

Like the ECE, the MCE is not a PSR and MCE is coordinate-dependent. We adapt the MCE to regression in the same way as the ECE.

Area under the retention curve (R-AUC)

The R-AUC [43] measures the usefulness of a model’s uncertainty estimates for selecting correct predictions. For varying certainty thresholds τ\tau, the retention curve tracks the error rate of a model when only predicting on the the subset with certainty at least τ\tau. When uncertainty is informative, incorrect predictions tend to be rejected first, resulting in a steep decline of the retention curve. By integrating this curve, R-AUC yields a single scalar that reflects both overall predictive accuracy and the ability of uncertainty estimates to rank errors. Formally, let si=s⁡(fi)s_{i}=s(f_{i}) denote a scalar uncertainty score for instance ii, with larger values indicating higher uncertainty. We use the predictive entropy,

si=−fi​log⁡fi−(1−fi)​log⁡(1−fi).s_{i}=-f_{i}\log f_{i}-(1-f_{i})\log(1-f_{i}).

Let π\pi be a permutation of {1,…,n}\{1,\dots,n\} s.t. sπ⁡(1)≥⋯≥sπ⁡(n)s_{\pi(1)}\geq\cdots\geq s_{\pi(n)}. For r∈{0,1,…,n}r\in\{0,1,\dots,n\}, define the retained index set

Rr:={π⁡(r+1),…,π⁡(n)},R_{r}:=\{\pi(r+1),\dots,\pi(n)\},

corresponding to retaining a fraction τ=|Rr|/n\tau=|R_{r}|/n of predictions and deferring the remaining rr most uncertain instances to an oracle. The area under the retention curve (R-AUC) is then defined as

R-AUC(𝒇,𝒚):=1n∑r=0n−1(1+Acc(𝒇i:i∈Rr,𝒚i:i∈Rr)),\text{R-AUC}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\bigl(1+\text{Acc}(\boldsymbol{f}_{i:i\in R_{r}},\boldsymbol{y}_{i:i\in R_{r}})\bigr),

where 1+Acc1+\text{Acc} is the error rate—remember that our Acc is the negative conventional accuracy. The R-AUC is not a PSR, since it can be improved by pushing uncertainty scores for likely-wrong predictions artificially high, so honest reporting is not necessarily optimal. Further, the R-AUC is coordinate-dependent: changing a single prediction fif_{i} affects not only the error term 𝟏fi≠yi\boldsymbol{1}_{f_{i}\neq y_{i}} associated with instance ii, but also the ordering induced by the uncertainty scores {sk}k=1n\{s_{k}\}_{k=1}^{n}.

For regression models, we use the Gaussian predictive entropy as uncertainty score and the MSE as error rate. Like in binary classification, the regression R-AUC is not a PSR and is coordinate-dependent.

Error detection (E-Det)

E-Det [44] evaluates how well uncertainty can be used as a score to discriminate between correct and incorrect predictions. We define the hard predictions as y^i=𝟏fi>0.5\hat{y}_{i}=\boldsymbol{1}_{f_{i}>0.5} and the corresponding error indicators as ei=𝟏y^i≠yie_{i}=\boldsymbol{1}_{\hat{y}_{i}\neq y_{i}}. Again writing sis_{i} for the uncertainty score (where we use predictive entropy, as above), E-Det is defined as the classical area under the receiver operating curve (AUROC), using sis_{i} as predictions for the labels eie_{i}. To conform with our notion that smaller metrics correspond to better performance, we consider the negative conventional error detection as our E-Det. The E-Det is not a PSR and the E-Det is coordinate-dependent because of its ranking characteristic, similar to the R-AUC.

In regression, we again use the Gaussian predictive entropy as uncertainty score and define errors eie_{i} as predictions whose relative errors |y−μ|y|+ε||\tfrac{y-\mu}{|y|+\varepsilon}| exceed 10%10\% (using a small ε>0\varepsilon>0 to ensure the relative error is well-defined).

Proposition F.1 (Coordinate-(in)dependence of common UQ evaluation metrics).

The NLL, BS, Acc, and MSE are coordinate-independent, and the ECE, MCE, R-AUC, and E-Det are coordinate-dependent.

Proof.

The coordinate-independence of the NLL, BS, Acc, and MSE follows directly from their pointwise-separability by definition. We now prove coordinate-dependence of the remaining metrics.

ECE & MCE: We prove the claim for ECE; the claim for MCE then follows by the same construction (indeed, in our construction, only one bin is populated, so ECE=MCE\text{ECE}=\text{MCE}).

Step 1: choose a rational frequency inside a non-degenerate bin. Let B=(ℓ,u]B=(\ell,u] be a bin of nonzero width, i.e., u−ℓ>0u-\ell>0. Pick any rational number q∈(ℓ,u)q\in(\ell,u); write it as q=k/tq=k/t with integers t≥2t\geq 2 and k∈{0,1,…,t}k\in\{0,1,\dots,t\}. (Existence is guaranteed since every non-degenerate interval contains rationals.) Set n:=tn:=t and fix labels 𝒚\boldsymbol{y} with exactly kk ones and t−kt-k zeros. Hence, for any prediction vector 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} for which all coordinates lie in BB, we have

freq⁡(B)=1t​∑i=1tyi=kt=q.\mathrm{freq}(B)=\frac{1}{t}\sum_{i=1}^{t}y_{i}=\frac{k}{t}=q.

Step 2: fix two values a<ba<b in the same bin. Choose any a,b∈Ba,b\in B with a<ba<b and with aa and bb sufficiently close to qq so that the values defined below remain inside BB. (Concretely: since BB is an open neighborhood of qq relative to (ℓ,u](\ell,u], there exists δ>0\delta>0 s.t. (q−δ,q+δ)⊆B(q-\delta,q+\delta)\subseteq B; choose a,b∈(q−δ,q+δ)a,b\in(q-\delta,q+\delta) with a<ba<b.) Fix an index i∈{1,…,t}i\in\{1,\dots,t\} (any choice works).

Step 3: build two backgrounds that make the direction of change flip. Define c:=t​q−at−1c:=\tfrac{tq-a}{t-1} and c′:=t​q−bt−1c^{\prime}:=\tfrac{tq-b}{t-1}. By construction, if we set all coordinates of 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} except ii equal to cc (respectively c′c^{\prime}), then the bin confidence equals qq when fi=af_{i}=a (respectively fi=bf_{i}=b):

1t​(a+∑r≠ic)=a+(t−1)​ct=a+t​q−at=q,1t​(b+∑r≠ic′)=b+(t−1)​c′t=q.\frac{1}{t}\Bigl(a+\sum_{r\neq i}c\Bigr)=\frac{a+(t-1)c}{t}=\frac{a+tq-a}{t}=q,\quad\frac{1}{t}\Bigl(b+\sum_{r\neq i}c^{\prime}\Bigr)=\frac{b+(t-1)c^{\prime}}{t}=q.

Since aa and bb were chosen sufficiently close to qq, the values cc and c′c^{\prime} are also close to qq and thus lie in BB as well (note that we can rewrite c,c′c,c^{\prime} as perturbations of qq: c=q+q−at−1c=q+\tfrac{q-a}{t-1}, c′=q+q−bt−1c^{\prime}=q+\tfrac{q-b}{t-1}. Therefore, in both constructions, all predictions fall into the same bin BB. Now define two prediction vectors:

𝒇1:=(a,c,…,c⏟t−1​ times),𝒇~1:=(b,c,…,c⏟t−1​ times),\boldsymbol{f}_{1}:=(a,\underbrace{c,\dots,c}_{t-1\text{ times}}),\qquad\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_{1}:=(b,\underbrace{c,\dots,c}_{t-1\text{ times}}),

and

𝒇2:=(a,c′,…,c′⏟t−1​ times),𝒇~2:=(b,c′,…,c′⏟t−1​ times),\boldsymbol{f}_{2}:=(a,\underbrace{c^{\prime},\dots,c^{\prime}}_{t-1\text{ times}}),\qquad\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_{2}:=(b,\underbrace{c^{\prime},\dots,c^{\prime}}_{t-1\text{ times}}),

where the distinguished coordinate is ii (we suppress the explicit placement notation for readability). Since all coordinates lie in BB, the ECE reduces to the single-bin absolute deviation:

ECE𝒚​(𝒇)=|freq⁡(B)−conf⁡(B)|.\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})=\bigl|\mathrm{freq}(B)-\mathrm{conf}(B)\bigr|.

For 𝒇1\boldsymbol{f}_{1} we have conf⁡(B)=q=freq⁡(B)\mathrm{conf}(B)=q=\mathrm{freq}(B), hence ECE𝒚​(𝒇1)=0\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{1})=0. But for 𝒇~1\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_{1} we have

conf⁡(B)=b+(t−1)​ct=b+(t​q−a)t=q+b−at,\mathrm{conf}(B)=\frac{b+(t-1)c}{t}=\frac{b+(tq-a)}{t}=q+\frac{b-a}{t},

so

ECE𝒚​(𝒇~1)=|q−(q+b−at)|=b−at>0.\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_{1})=\Bigl|q-\Bigl(q+\frac{b-a}{t}\Bigr)\Bigr|=\frac{b-a}{t}>0.

Thus, under the background 𝒓=(c,…,c)\boldsymbol{r}=(c,\dots,c), changing fif_{i} from aa to bb increases the ECE: ECE𝒚​((a,𝒓))<ECE𝒚​((b,𝒓))\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl((a,\boldsymbol{r})\bigr)<\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl((b,\boldsymbol{r})\bigr). Conversely, for 𝒇~2\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_{2} we again have perfect calibration in BB by construction, hence ECE𝒚​(𝒇~2)=0\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\tilde{\boldsymbol{f}}_{2})=0, whereas for 𝒇2\boldsymbol{f}_{2} we compute

conf⁡(B)=a+(t−1)​c′t=a+(t​q−b)t=q−b−at,\mathrm{conf}(B)=\frac{a+(t-1)c^{\prime}}{t}=\frac{a+(tq-b)}{t}=q-\frac{b-a}{t},

so

ECE𝒚​(𝒇2)=|q−(q−b−at)|=b−at>0.\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f}_{2})=\Bigl|q-\Bigl(q-\frac{b-a}{t}\Bigr)\Bigr|=\frac{b-a}{t}>0.

Hence, under the background 𝒓′=(c′,…,c′)\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}=(c^{\prime},\dots,c^{\prime}), changing fif_{i} from aa to bb decreases the ECE: ECE𝒚​((a,𝒓′))>ECE𝒚​((b,𝒓′))\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl((a,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})\bigr)>\text{ECE}_{\boldsymbol{y}}\bigl((b,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})\bigr).

Transfer to regression. Fix a nominal level α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). For Gaussian predictive distributions, let

α^((𝝁,𝝈2),𝒚):=1n∑i=1n𝟏{yi∉Iα(μi,σi2)}\hat{\alpha}((\boldsymbol{\mu},\boldsymbol{\sigma}^{2}),\boldsymbol{y}):=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\boldsymbol{1}_{\{y_{i}\notin I_{\alpha}(\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2})\}}

denote the empirical miscoverage of the (1−α)(1-\alpha)-level prediction interval Iα​(μi,σi2)I_{\alpha}(\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}). Since the regression ECE (resp. MCE) is obtained by averaging (resp. maximizing) the absolute deviations |α^−α|\lvert\hat{\alpha}-\alpha\rvert over the finitely many levels αj\alpha_{j}, coordinate-independence would in particular require coordinate-independence of the contribution of each fixed level α\alpha (as we can easily pick labels and predictions such that slightly perturbing a prediction only affects one miscoverage term). We therefore fix α\alpha and construct a counterexample for |α^−α|\lvert\hat{\alpha}-\alpha\rvert. As in the classification proof, fix an index ii and two alternative predictions aa and bb for the iith coordinate (i.e., two Gaussian reports (μi,σi2)(\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2})), such that the iith prediction interval covers yiy_{i} under aa but does not cover yiy_{i} under bb. For the remaining coordinates k≠ik\neq i, construct two background prediction vectors 𝒓\boldsymbol{r} and 𝒓′\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime} as follows: in 𝒓\boldsymbol{r}, choose the (μk,σk2)(\mu_{k},\sigma_{k}^{2}) so that exactly α​t\alpha t of the t−1t-1 background prediction intervals fail to cover their labels when the iith coordinate is set to aa, whereas in 𝒓′\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}, choose them so that exactly α​t\alpha t background intervals fail to cover their labels when the iith coordinate is set to bb (such constructions are always possible by choosing the remaining intervals sufficiently wide or narrow.). By construction, we then have

α^​((a,𝒓),𝒚)=α,α^​((b,𝒓′),𝒚)=α,\hat{\alpha}((a,\boldsymbol{r}),\boldsymbol{y})=\alpha,\quad\hat{\alpha}((b,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}),\boldsymbol{y})=\alpha,

so that |α^−α|=0\lvert\hat{\alpha}-\alpha\rvert=0 in both cases. However, switching aa to bb under the background 𝒓\boldsymbol{r} increases the number of miscovered instances by one and thus increases |α^−α|\lvert\hat{\alpha}-\alpha\rvert, whereas switching aa to bb under the background 𝒓′\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime} decreases the number of miscovered instances by one and thus decreases |α^−α|\lvert\hat{\alpha}-\alpha\rvert. Hence,

|α^​((a,𝒓),𝒚)−α|<|α^​((b,𝒓),𝒚)−α|,|α^​((a,𝒓′),𝒚)−α|>|α^​((b,𝒓′),𝒚)−α|.\lvert\hat{\alpha}((a,\boldsymbol{r}),\boldsymbol{y})-\alpha\rvert<\lvert\hat{\alpha}((b,\boldsymbol{r}),\boldsymbol{y})-\alpha\rvert,\quad\lvert\hat{\alpha}((a,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}),\boldsymbol{y})-\alpha\rvert>\lvert\hat{\alpha}((b,\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime}),\boldsymbol{y})-\alpha\rvert.

This flip of inequalities shows that the direction of change of the calibration error induced by modifying a single coordinate depends on the remaining coordinates. Therefore, the regression ECE is coordinate-dependent. Moreover, by choosing a nominal level α\alpha whose absolute miscoverage deviation strictly dominates all others, the same construction ensures that this level uniquely attains the maximum in the definition of the regression MCE. Hence, the same argument applies to the regression MCE, which is therefore also coordinate-dependent.

Appendix G Generalization to the multiclass and multivariate setting

The purpose of this appendix is to demonstrate that our framework extends beyond the binary and univariate setting. We perform the analysis on three metrics and one utility each. Analogous results for additional metrics and decision families can be derived using the same template.

G.1 Multiclass classification

We consider probabilistic KK-class classification models, K>2K>2, f:𝒳→ΔK−1f:\mathcal{X}\to\Delta^{K-1}, mapping from the input space 𝒳\mathcal{X} to the (K−1)(K{-}1)-simplex ΔK−1:={p∈[0,1]K:∑j=1Kpj=1}\Delta^{K-1}:=\{p\in[0,1]^{K}:\sum_{j=1}^{K}p^{j}=1\}, so the prediction for an instance is f=(f1,…,fK)f=(f^{1},\ldots,f^{K}) with fjf^{j} denoting the predicted probability that the true label y∈𝒴:=[K]:={1,…,K}y\in\mathcal{Y}:=[K]:=\{1,\ldots,K\} equals jj.

As evaluation metrics, we consider the multiclass NLL, BS, and ECE. We define

NLL⁡(𝒇,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1n(−log⁡fiyi),BS⁡(𝒇,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1n∑j=1K(fij−𝟏yi=j)2.\mathrm{NLL}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(-\log f_{i}^{y_{i}}\bigr),\quad\mathrm{BS}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\bigl(f_{i}^{j}-\boldsymbol{1}_{y_{i}=j}\bigr)^{2}.

The multiclass ECE uses the standard extension to vector-valued predictions via one-versus-all binning (see, e.g., [45]). The NLL and BS are pointwise-separable (hence coordinate-independent) by definition. The multiclass ECE is coordinate-dependent by the same bin-coupling argument as in the binary case (Proposition F.1).

As downstream task, we generalize the binary decision from Section 3.2.1 to multiclass via a one-vs-rest decomposition. For each class j∈[K]j\in[K], we consider the binary decision “flag instance as class jj or not,” with cost threshold c∈(0,1)c\in(0,1). Defining the binary label y~j:=𝟏y=j\tilde{y}^{j}:=\boldsymbol{1}_{y=j}, the Bayes act is to flag class jj whenever fj>cf^{j}>c. The pointwise utility of a prediction ff with true label yy for class jj at threshold cc is

uj,c​(f,y)=−y~j​(1−c)​𝟏fj≤c−(1−y~j)​c​𝟏fj>c.u_{j,c}(f,y)=-\tilde{y}^{j}(1-c)\boldsymbol{1}_{f^{j}\leq c}-(1-\tilde{y}^{j})c\boldsymbol{1}_{f^{j}>c}.

This is exactly the binary utility ucu_{c} from Section 3.2.1, applied to the binary prediction–label pair (fj,y~j)(f^{j},\tilde{y}^{j}). The combined decision family is indexed by θ=(j,c)∈[K]×(0,1)\theta=(j,c)\in[K]\times(0,1), with dataset-level utility Uj,c​(𝒇,𝒚)=1n​∑i=1nuj,c​(fi,yi)U_{j,c}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_{j,c}(f_{i},y_{i}). In particular, Uj,cU_{j,c} is pointwise-separable.

Proposition G.1.

The multiclass NLL and BS are decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uj,c}j∈[K],c∈(0,1)\{U_{j,c}\}_{j\in[K],c\in(0,1)} with πNLL​(j,c)=1/c\pi_{\mathrm{NLL}}(j,c)=1/c and πBS​(j,c)=2\pi_{\mathrm{BS}}(j,c)=2, and h𝐲=idh_{\boldsymbol{y}}=\mathrm{id} for all 𝐲\boldsymbol{y}.

Proof.

NLL: Evaluating the per-instance expected negative utility under π⁡(j,c)=1/c\pi(j,c)=1/c gives

∑j=1K∫01−uj,c(fi,yi)1cdc\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{K}\int_{0}^{1}-u_{j,c}(f_{i},y_{i})\,\frac{1}{c}\;\mathrm{d}c =∫fiyi11−cc​𝑑c+∑j≠yi∫0fij1​𝑑c\displaystyle=\int_{f_{i}^{y_{i}}}^{1}\frac{1-c}{c}\;\mathrm{d}c+\sum_{j\neq y_{i}}\int_{0}^{f_{i}^{j}}1\;\mathrm{d}c
=[−log⁡fiyi−1+fiyi]+∑j≠yifij\displaystyle=\bigl[-\log f_{i}^{y_{i}}-1+f_{i}^{y_{i}}\bigr]+\sum_{j\neq y_{i}}f_{i}^{j}
=−log⁡fiyi−1+fiyi+(1−fiyi)=−log⁡fiyi.\displaystyle=-\log f_{i}^{y_{i}}-1+f_{i}^{y_{i}}+(1-f_{i}^{y_{i}})=-\log f_{i}^{y_{i}}.

In the last step we used the simplex constraint ∑j≠yifij=1−fiyi\sum_{j\neq y_{i}}f_{i}^{j}=1-f_{i}^{y_{i}}. Averaging over instances, EU𝒚​(𝒇)=NLL⁡(𝒇,𝒚)\mathrm{EU}_{\boldsymbol{y}}(\boldsymbol{f})=\mathrm{NLL}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}), so the NLL is decision-aligned with h𝒚=idh_{\boldsymbol{y}}=\mathrm{id}.

BS: The multiclass BS decomposes as BS⁡(𝒇,𝒚)=∑j=1KBS(j)​(𝒇,𝒚)\mathrm{BS}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\mathrm{BS}^{(j)}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}), where BS(j)​(𝒇,𝒚)\mathrm{BS}^{(j)}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) is the binary BS for the jj-th one-vs-rest problem. By Proposition 3.7, each binary BS admits the integral representation (3) with prior π⁡(c)=2\pi(c)=2, giving BS(𝒇,𝒚)=∑j=1K∫01−Uj,c(𝒇,𝒚)⋅2dc\mathrm{BS}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})=\sum_{j=1}^{K}\int_{0}^{1}-U_{j,c}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y})\cdot 2\;\mathrm{d}c, which matches Definition 3.1 with h𝒚=idh_{\boldsymbol{y}}=\mathrm{id}.

∎

As in the binary case, the NLL and BS implicit priors are pathological. The ECE is not decision-aligned as a direct consequence of Lemma 3.6.

Corollary G.2.

The multiclass ECE is not decision-aligned w.r.t. {Uj,c}j∈[K],c∈(0,1)\{U_{j,c}\}_{j\in[K],c\in(0,1)}.

G.2 Multivariate regression

We consider probabilistic multivariate regression models with output dimension D>1D>1. We assume a Gaussian predictive distribution and consider models of the form f:𝒳→ℝD×𝕊+⁣+Df:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}^{D}\times\mathbb{S}^{D}_{++}, mapping from the input space 𝒳\mathcal{X} to the predictive mean μ∈ℝD\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and predictive covariance Σ∈𝕊+⁣+D\Sigma\in\mathbb{S}^{D}_{++} (the cone of D×DD\times D symmetric positive definite matrices), so f=(μ,Σ)f=(\mu,\Sigma). The regression target is y∈𝒴:=ℝDy\in\mathcal{Y}:=\mathbb{R}^{D}.

As evaluation metrics, we consider the multivariate NLL, MSE, and the energy score (ES) [9].1515 15 To the best of our knowledge, there is no established notion of the ECE for multivariate regression. Therefore, we consider the ES, which is a more established metric in this context. We define

NLL⁡(𝒇,𝒚)\displaystyle\mathrm{NLL}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) =1n​∑i=1n[D2​log⁡(2​π)+12​log​det(Σi)+12​(yi−μi)⊤​Σi−1​(yi−μi)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\frac{D}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac{1}{2}\log\det(\Sigma_{i})+\frac{1}{2}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})^{\top}\Sigma_{i}^{-1}(y_{i}-\mu_{i})\right],
MSE⁡(𝒇,𝒚)\displaystyle\mathrm{MSE}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) =1n​∑i=1n‖yi−μi‖2.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|y_{i}-\mu_{i}\|^{2}.

For a predictive distribution ff and observation yy, the per-instance ES is defined as

les​(f,y)=𝔼X∼f​‖X−y‖−12​𝔼X,X′∼f​‖X−X′‖,l_{\mathrm{es}}(f,y)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim f}\|X-y\|-\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_{X,X^{\prime}\sim f}\|X-X^{\prime}\|,

where X,X′X,X^{\prime} are independent draws from ff and ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm, and the dataset-level ES is the average. All three metrics are pointwise-separable by definition.

As downstream task, we generalize selective prediction from Section 3.3.1 to multivariate output by applying the univariate selective-prediction rule coordinate-wise to each standardized output dimension and averaging over dimensions. Concretely, for each output dimension d∈[D]d\in[D] the decision-maker chooses an action in {predict,abstain}\{\text{predict},\text{abstain}\}. To put dimensions of different scale on equal footing, costs are standardized by the marginal variance vd:=Var⁡(yd)v_{d}:=\mathrm{Var}(y_{d}), so the standardized squared-error loss for a point prediction in dimension dd is (yd−μd)2/vd(y_{d}-\mu_{d})^{2}/v_{d}, and the abstention cost is a dimensionless λ∈ℝ>0\lambda\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}. Equivalently, this is the univariate selective-prediction problem of Section 3.3.1 applied independently to each of the standardized targets yd/vdy_{d}/\sqrt{v_{d}}.1616 16 Note that we apply the same scaling in the univariate case (see Appendix I), but we omitted this notation in the main text for brevity. The Bayes act in dimension dd is to predict μd\mu_{d} whenever the standardized predictive variance Σd​d/vd\Sigma_{dd}/v_{d} is at most λ\lambda. The pointwise utility of a prediction f=(μ,Σ)f=(\mu,\Sigma) with true outcome y∈ℝDy\in\mathbb{R}^{D} is

uλ(f,y)=−1D∑d=1D[(yd−μd)2vd 1Σd​d≤λ​vd+λ 1Σd​d>λ​vd].u_{\lambda}(f,y)=-\frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D}\left[\frac{(y_{d}-\mu_{d})^{2}}{v_{d}}\,\boldsymbol{1}_{\Sigma_{dd}\leq\lambda v_{d}}+\lambda\,\boldsymbol{1}_{\Sigma_{dd}>\lambda v_{d}}\right].

The dataset-level utility Uλ​(𝒇,𝒚)U_{\lambda}(\boldsymbol{f},\boldsymbol{y}) is defined as the average pointwise utility. In particular, UλU_{\lambda} is pointwise-separable.
